synopsis: The research used documented cases to judge what a team starting from zero in October 2026 could achieve by mid-2027, without internal machine recordings, site video, sensor specifications or documents; missing evidence had to be reported as “not found,” not replaced with estimates [f296, f7, f302]. Important claims were to distinguish independent evidence, vendor claims and expert opinion, report failures as well as successes, and explicitly mark on-road evidence because its transfer to off-road machines is an inference [f1191, f1193, f10402]. The off-road evidence base remains thin: a 2022 NIOSH review covered 64 articles from 2000–2020 and 97 haul-truck collision-system cases, yet mining intervention evidence is low-maturity, independent field data are old and sparse, and no peer-reviewed synthetic-only demonstration of heavy-machine collision-avoidance reliability was found [f5933, f5932, f5169, f6690]. Accident statistics establish the importance of mobile-machine risk rather than the fraction automatic braking could address, while near-miss under-reporting and unmeasured braking-created risks limit conclusions [f2982, f3007, f3025, f3046]. No reviewed excerpts of ISO 21815 or ISO 17757:2019, confirmed in 2024, set simulation-evidence rules, and no regulator acceptance of off-road virtual evidence was found; the FAA provides a published compliance example, while FDA credibility guidance makes evidence adequacy risk- and context-dependent rather than prescribing a universal physical-test minimum [f3908, f5215, f7619, f7642, f7646]. Programme work packages should therefore specify the safety evidence they must produce, organized into a safety case, with simulation directing scarce physical-test time and multiplying evidence rather than replacing physical tests [f9398, f11298, f11311].
